The article's PBX example is why a CPaaS trunk and a customer's own extension list are different attestation problems. Source date: 2026-10.
docs.eg: Wikipedia says STIR/SHAKEN is a suite of protocols and procedures intended to combat caller ID spoofing.

docs.ti: 10DLC is a name on the compliance pages
docs.ex: Treat 10DLC as a registration topic you saw named, not as a rule you finished reading. Twilio's page is a map of brand and campaign objects. Sinch's docs list an API with the same words, brand and campaign. Neither page, in the text this session kept, defined the acronym or priced the registration. Source date: 2026-10.
docs.eg: Twilio's compliance page that opened is titled Programmable Messaging and A2P 10DLC.

docs.ti: Two domains and a SIP trunk
docs.ex: Draw two clouds before you draw a price. Private is the PBX side. Public is the telephone network side. The trunk is the interconnection the article requires between them. Twilio and Telnyx are two providers whose trunk pages opened. Their field names are not the same. Source date: 2026-10.
docs.eg: Wikipedia says SIP trunking is how Internet telephony service providers deliver telephone services to customers with a SIP-based IP-PBX.

docs.ex: Read Basic and Enhanced as different products on Twilio's own page. Enhanced sends the number and the address. Basic does not. The national call center is the fallback the page describes when the number has neither. That is a Twilio sentence. It is not a description of Bandwidth and not a statute. Source date: 2026-10.
docs.eg: Twilio's SIP trunking emergency page says the feature routes emergency calls to PSAPs in the US, Canada, the UK, Australia, Ireland, France, Germany, and Austria.

docs.ti: Twilio and Vonage, from the articles
docs.ex: Use the articles for the company and the product family, not for this month's invoice. Twilio's story on the page is an API company: voice in 2008, messaging in 2010, later Authy and SendGrid. The breach years are a reason this lab never stores a credential. They are not a configuration step. Source date: 2026-10.
docs.eg: Wikipedia calls Twilio an American cloud communications company based in San Francisco that provides programmable tools for phone calls, text messages, and other functions using web service APIs.

docs.ti: TwiML verbs and what an IVR is
docs.ex: An IVR, in the encyclopedia, gathers and routes. TwiML is one vendor's XML for telling Twilio what to do on a call. Say speaks. Play plays a file. Gather collects input. Dial, Queue, and Conference move the call. Hangup and Reject end it. Pay is a payment verb on that list. None of those words is a contact-center workforce plan. Source date: 2026-10.
docs.eg: Wikipedia says an IVR interacts with callers, gathers information, and routes calls, using speech recognition and DTMF from the keypad.

docs.ti: Where the vendors put the same words
docs.ex: Two vendors use the words. Twilio has a trusted-calling title and an onboarding label. Bandwidth has an API sentence and a separate caller-name query for the US and Canada. CNAM and STIR are neighbors, not the same API. The caller-name service tells you a name. STIR tells you how strongly a provider asserts the number. Source date: 2026-10.
docs.eg: Twilio's voice docs include a page titled Trusted calling with SHAKEN/STIR, and the voice navigation lists SHAKEN/STIR overview and onboarding beside Voice Integrity.

docs.ti: Voice and video names that opened
docs.ex: Count products, not features you hope are included. Twilio Video is a docs set with three named client quickstarts. Vonage lists Video beside Voice. This session did not open a Vonage video overview paragraph, so Vonage video details stay at the navigation level. Source date: 2026-10.
docs.eg: Twilio's docs home lists Programmable Voice, Programmable Messaging, Verify, Video, Elastic SIP Trunking, and Conversations among its products.

docs.ex: Direction is the whole lesson. Your POST to the vendor creates or asks. The vendor's HTTP request to you is the event. Mixing them up looks like a timeout when you are waiting on the wrong side. Source date: 2026-10.
docs.eg: Twilio's webhook introduction says Twilio uses webhooks to notify your web app when events such as incoming calls or SMS messages occur.

SIP, WebRTC, RTP, numbers, messaging, STIR/SHAKEN, emergency calling, webhooks, IVR, contact center, AI voice, and migration. A number that was not on an opened page is marked confirm.
